method.name: Flash Flood Potential Index (FFPI)
method.summary: Each 30 m square is rated 1 to 10 for slope (M), land cover (L), soil (S) and bare ground (V); the four are weighted as in the paper's Scenario 2 and rounded to 0.1. Higher means water runs off faster and gathers sooner after heavy rain. Classes follow the paper's reading of 5 to 6 as medium: low under 4.5, high from 6.5, extreme from 8.5.

factors.M: Slope: from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface after taking the lowest height of each 3 x 3 squares (about 90 m) to drop most roofs and trees. 3 % or less rates 1, each further 3 % one more, above 27 % rates 10 (the paper's table leaves 27-30 % out; its 3 % steps are continued).
factors.L: Land cover: ESA WorldCover 2021 (10 m) in each square, rated with the paper's table: water 1, wetland and mangrove 2, tree cover 3 (plantations included), shrubland 5, grassland and cropland 6, bare ground 7. A square at least a fifth built-up rates by its built-up share, as the US land cover database the table comes from sorts developed land: 80 % or more 10, 50-79 % 9, 20-49 % 8; under a fifth, built-up pixels count as developed open space (7) and the square takes the mean.
factors.S: Soil: SoilGrids 2.0 sand, silt and clay in the top 15 cm, sorted into a USDA texture class and rated with the paper's table (silty clay, which the table leaves out, rates 9 like clay). SoilGrids has no value under towns; there the square's built-up share counts as impervious (10) and the rest takes the nearest SoilGrids value.
factors.V: Vegetation: the share of ground under plants from the 2021 Sentinel-2 NDVI composite (median), ((NDVI - 0.2) / (0.86 - 0.2)) squared, averaged over the square. 90-100 % rates 1, each 10 % less one more, under 10 % rates 10.

method.classes: Four classes, as the paper names them; it gives no limits but reads Scenario 2 scores of 5 to 6 as medium, so medium runs from 4.5 to under 6.5 (5 and 6 once rounded): low below 4.5, medium from 4.5, high from 6.5, extreme from 8.5. A score on a limit is in the class above.
citations: Smith, G. (2003). Flash flood potential: determining the hydrologic response of FFMP basins to heavy rain by analyzing their physiographic characteristics. NOAA National Weather Service, Colorado Basin River Forecast Center.
Mohd Yassin, N. A., Adnan, N. A. and Md Sadek, E. S. S. (2023). Analysis of Flash Flood Potential Index (FFPI) and scenarios assessment in Shah Alam using GIS approach. Planning Malaysia 21(2).
Carlson, T. N. and Ripley, D. A. (1997). On the relation between NDVI, fractional vegetation cover, and leaf area index. Remote Sensing of Environment 62(3): 241-252.
Horn, B. K. P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69(1): 14-47.
deviations: Land cover is ESA WorldCover 2021, not the US land cover database the rating table was written for; developed intensity comes from each square's built-up share.
Slopes of 27-30 %, which the paper leaves unrated, rate 10.
Silty clay, missing from the soil table, rates 9 like clay.
Where SoilGrids has no value (under towns), the built-up share counts as impervious and the rest takes the nearest SoilGrids value.
Vegetation cover comes from NDVI (Carlson and Ripley's scaled NDVI squared), not from a mapped percentage.
The surface model includes roofs and trees; taking the lowest height of each 3 x 3 squares before the slope removes most of them, not all.
The paper gives no class limits; as it reads scores of 5 to 6 as medium, the limits here are 4.5, 6.5 and 8.5.
method.not: A susceptibility to flash floods, not a water depth and not a chance of flooding. Drains, their size and upkeep, which decide most town flash floods, are not in it.
